en: Peṭakopadesa:
Exposition of Miscellaneous Topics.
Jhāna is dispassion (virāga).
The four jhānas should be treated in detail.
They are of two kinds:
those dissociated from the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) and those associated with the factors of enlightenment.

In that regard, those dissociated from the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) belong to outsiders, while those associated with the factors of enlightenment belong to noble persons (ariya-puggala). Therein, having set aside the six bases for persons— namely,

the person of lustful temperament (rāga-carita), the person of hateful temperament (dosa-carita), the person of deluded temperament (moha-carita), the person of both lustful and hateful temperament (rāga-dosa-carita),

the person of both lustful and deluded temperament (rāga-moha-carita), the person of both hateful and deluded temperament (dosa-moha-carita), and the person of balanced temperament (samabhāga-carita)— of these persons...
For those who have attained jhāna, the five hindrances are the adversaries;
since it is incapable of suppressing them [directly], it suppresses the three unwholesome roots.

Through the unwholesome root of greed, covetousness and agitation—which are states of restlessness—are suppressed by the wholesome root of non-greed. Regret and doubt belong to the side of delusion; these are suppressed by non-delusion.
Ill will and sloth-and-torpor belong to the side of hatred; he subdues them with non-hatred.
Therein, for the fulfillment of non-greed, he directs thoughts of renunciation.
Therein, for the fulfillment of non-hatred, he directs thoughts of non-ill will.
Therein, for the fulfillment of non-delusion, he directs his thoughts toward thoughts of non-harming.
Therein, for the fulfillment of non-greed, he is secluded from sensual pleasures.

Therein, through the fulfillment of non-hatred and the fulfillment of non-delusion, he is secluded from evil, unwholesome states; with directed thought and evaluation, born of seclusion, filled with rapture and pleasure, he enters and dwells in the first jhāna.
Thoughts (vitakka) are three types of thoughts:
the thought of renunciation, the thought of non-ill will, and the thought of non-cruelty.
Therein, the initial application [of the mind] is thought; the sustained wandering of that which has been attained is examination (vicāra).

Just as a man sees a person coming from afar and does not yet know whether it is a woman or a man, but when he discerns whether it is a woman or a man, or of such a complexion or of such a shape, he further examines it while reflecting:
"Is this person virtuous or immoral? Is he wealthy or poor?"
In this way, investigation (vicāra) applies itself to initial application (vitakka); investigation moves about and follows along.

Just as a bird first gathers its feathers and afterwards does not gather them, so is initial application; just as the spreading out of the wings, so is investigation. It protects, it applies itself, it moves about, it investigates.
It thinks, it applies itself; it moves about following along, it investigates.

Applied thought (*vitakka*) is the antidote to the perception of sensual desire (*kāmasaññā*); sustained thought (*vicāra*) is the antidote to the perception of ill will (*byāpādasaññā*) and the perception of cruelty (*vihiṁsasaññā*).
The function of applied thoughts is the non-attention to the unwholesome; the function of sustained thoughts is the restraint of the preeminent [defilements].
Just as a reciter repeats his lesson in silence, so is applied thought; just as he reflects upon that very same [lesson], so is sustained thought.
Just as non-penetration is, so is applied thought (vitakka).
Just as penetration is, so is sustained thought (vicāra).

In the analytical knowledge of language (nirutti-patisambhidā) and the analytical knowledge of eloquence (paṭibhāna-patisambhidā), there is applied thought; in the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dhamma-patisambhidā) and the analytical knowledge of meaning (attha-patisambhidā), there is sustained thought.
Skillfulness of the mind is applied thought (*vitakka*); skillfulness in directing the mind is sustained thought (*vicāra*). "This is wholesome, this is unwholesome;
this is to be developed, this is to be abandoned, this is to be realized"—this is applied thought. Just as there is abandoning, developing, and realizing, so too is sustained thought.
For one established in these applied and sustained thoughts, two kinds of suffering do not arise: neither bodily nor mental.
Two kinds of happiness arise: bodily and mental.
Thus, the mental happiness born of applied thought is rapture (*pīti*); the bodily happiness is purely bodily.
That one-pointedness of mind therein is concentration (*samādhi*).
Thus, the first jhāna is characterized by the abandoning of five factors and the possession of five factors.
Through the constant cultivation of those very same applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), his mind becomes inclined toward them;
consequently, applied thought and sustained thought appear gross to him.
And whatever joy and pleasure there is, as well as the renunciation, becomes gross;
moreover, joy and delight born of concentration arise.
Its object is sustained thought (*vicāra*).
With their subsiding, his mind becomes tranquil within.
Those two states—initial application and sustained application—are to be recollected;
the present ones are to be seen as a tearing apart.
With their subsiding, there is singleness and one-pointedness of mind.
Through that singleness, rapture reaches fulfillment.
That which is rapture is the faculty of mental joy; that which is pleasure is the faculty of physical pleasure.
That which is one-pointedness of mind is concentration.
That second jhāna is endowed with four factors.
Through the fading away of rapture, he dwells having abandoned the mire accompanied by passion.
In that regard, while discerning that "the mind accompanied by joy is clinging," he attends only to equanimity.
With the fading away of rapture, he dwells in equanimity;
and he experiences with the body that pleasure which was previously sought through rapture, dwelling in full awareness.
By means of that mindfulness and clear comprehension, one reaches the fulfillment of equanimity.
This is the third jhāna, endowed with four factors.
Likewise, through the abandoning of bodily pleasure, the faculty of mental joy ceases in the first jhāna.
In the second jhāna, the faculty of pain ceases.

With the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.
Therein, equanimity is clarity by way of four faculties: the faculty of pain, the faculty of grief, the faculty of pleasure, and the faculty of joy.
With the cessation of those [two], there is equanimity and clear comprehension; therein, due to the faculty of pleasure and the faculty of mental joy, there is non-remembrance.
With the cessation of those, one becomes mindful. Due to the faculty of pain and the faculty of mental grief, there is lack of clear comprehension;
with the cessation of those, there is clear comprehension. Thus, there is perception associated with equanimity, mindfulness, clear comprehension, and one-pointedness of mind.
And this is called the fourth jhāna.
In that regard, for a person of lustful temperament, there is the faculty of pleasure and the faculty of mental joy;
for a person of hateful temperament, there is the faculty of pain and the faculty of mental grief.
For a person of deluded temperament, there is both lack of mindfulness and lack of clear comprehension.
In this regard, for a person of lustful temperament, attachment ceases in the third and fourth jhānas;
for a person of hateful temperament, aversion ceases in the first and second jhānas; and for a person of deluded temperament, [it ceases] in the first jhāna.
In the second [jhāna], lack of clear comprehension ceases;
in the third and fourth jhānas, non-attention ceases. In this very way, the four jhānas will reach purification for those three types of persons.
In that regard, for a person of lustful-and-hateful temperament, there is both lack of clear comprehension and both approval and resistance; therefore, their jhāna partakes of decline.
In that regard, for a person of lustful and deluded temperament, the showing of both attachment and danger constitutes for him meditation partaking of decline.

In that regard, for a person of irascible and deluded temperament, the showing of both aversion, lack of mindfulness, and lack of clear comprehension constitutes for him meditation partaking of decline.

In that regard, for a person of balanced temperament characterized by lust, hatred, and delusion, there is meditation partaking of distinction. These four meditations are to be demonstrated with respect to these seven types of persons.

Among the four concentrations: through concentration of desire comes the first jhāna; through concentration of energy, the second jhāna; through concentration of mind, the third jhāna; and through concentration of investigation, the fourth jhāna. Through the wishless comes the first jhāna;
through emptiness, the second jhāna; through the signless, the third jhāna; and through mindfulness of breathing, the fourth jhāna.
Through the subsiding of sensual thoughts and ill will, there is the first jhāna; through the subsiding of applied and sustained thought...
The second jhāna by means of tranquility; the third jhāna by means of the subsiding of the faculty of pleasure and the faculty of mental joy;
and the fourth jhāna by means of the subsiding of bodily formations.

The first jhāna through the foundation of relinquishment; the second jhāna through the foundation of truth; the third jhāna through the foundation of wisdom; and the fourth jhāna through the foundation of peace.
These four jhānas have been explained by way of a concise exposition; therein, the faculty of concentration reaches its fulfillment.

There are four corresponding [faculties]: herein, he who attains the destruction of the taints (*āsava*) by relying on the first jhāna does so by means of the pleasant path of slow direct knowledge, as the antidote to the faculty of mental distress (*domanassindriya*).

He who attains the destruction of the taints by relying on the second jhāna does so by means of the pleasant path of quick direct knowledge, as the antidote to the faculty of physical pain (*dukkhindriya*).
He who, by relying on the third jhāna, attains the destruction of the taints (āsava), has proceeded by a pleasant way with sluggish direct knowledge, as a counteragent to the faculty of mental joy.
He who, by relying on the fourth jhāna, attains the destruction of the taints, has proceeded by a pleasant way with swift direct knowledge, as a counteragent to the faculty of pleasure.
This concludes the miscellaneous exposition.
